deck: 40 Effective Java::09-10 General Programming and Exceptions

cards.front: Effective Java Item 57 — what is the rule for local variable scope?
cards.back: Declare each variable where it is first used, and keep its scope minimal
cards.extra: A variable declared at the top lives too long — it can be misused after the block that needed it, and the reader has to hold it in mind for no reason.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::07 Variables and Scopes
cards.example:
class LocalScope {
    void f(java.util.List xs) {
        for (String s : xs) { int len = s.length(); System.out.println(len); } // declared at first use
        // len is not visible here: minimal scope
    }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 58 — why prefer for-each to an indexed or iterator loop?
cards.back: It hides the index/iterator, so there is no off-by-one and no ConcurrentModificationException from misuse
cards.extra: The book: if you need the index or to remove, use a plain loop deliberately — not by default.
cards.example:
java.util.List<String> xs = new java.util.ArrayList<>(java.util.List.of("a", "b"));
for (int i = 0; i <= xs.size(); i++) System.out.println(xs.get(i));
for (String s : xs) System.out.println(s);
for (java.util.Iterator<String> it = xs.iterator(); it.hasNext();) { xs.remove(it.next()); }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 59 — what should you do before writing a utility method?
cards.back: Check whether the libraries already have it — and use theirs
cards.extra: The book's example: Math.abs(rnd.nextInt()) % n is biased and can return negative values; Random.nextInt(n) is correct. Library code is tested and improves over time.
cards.example:
class UseLibraries {
    static String reverse(String s) { return new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString(); } // use library
    static int max(java.util.List xs) { return java.util.Collections.max(xs); } // do not reinvent
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 60 — why are float and double unsuitable for money?
cards.back: They cannot represent decimal fractions exactly — 0.1 has no finite binary form
cards.extra: Use BigDecimal, int cents or long for exact values. Binary floating point is for measurement, not accounting.
cards.example:
double a = 0.1 + 0.2;
System.out.println(a);
java.math.BigDecimal b = new java.math.BigDecimal("0.10").add(new java.math.BigDecimal("0.20"));
System.out.println(b);

cards.front: Effective Java Item 61 — what are the three problems with boxed primitives?
cards.back: Identity comparisons are unreliable, unboxing null throws, and they cost memory and time
cards.extra: Integer a = 1000, b = 1000; a == b is false. Primitives have none of these traps.
cards.example:
class BoxingProblems { void f() {
    Integer a = 1000, b = 1000;
    System.out.println(a == b); // identity comparison unreliable
    Integer n = null; int x = n; // unboxing null throws; boxing costs memory and time
} }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 62 — when is a String the wrong type?
cards.back: For values with their own type — numbers, enums, aggregates, booleans
cards.extra: Parsing happens at every use, validation is lost, and the compiler cannot help. A String for a phone number is a String for every future bug.
cards.example:
record Point(int x, int y) {}
enum Color { RED, GREEN }
class TypedValues {
    int n = 42; Color c = Color.RED; boolean ok = true; Point p = new Point(1, 2); // number, enum, boolean, aggregate, not Strings
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 63 — what does the compiler actually do with + in a loop?
cards.back: Builds a StringBuilder per iteration (or creates a new String each time) — quadratic cost
cards.extra: Hoist one StringBuilder outside the loop, or use String.join. The operator is fine for a single expression, not for accumulation.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::01 Foundations::09 Strings and Methods
cards.example:
String s = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) s = s + "x";
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) sb.append("x");

cards.front: Effective Java Item 64 — what type should variables, parameters and return types use?
cards.back: The most general interface that serves the purpose — List, not ArrayList
cards.extra: Only the constructor needs the concrete class. Declaring the interface keeps the implementation swappable.
cards.example:
class GeneralTypes {
    static java.util.List copy(java.util.List in) { // List, not ArrayList
        return new java.util.ArrayList<>(in);
    }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 65 — why prefer interfaces to reflection?
cards.back: Reflection loses compile-time checking, is verbose, and is slower — mistakes become runtime errors
cards.extra: Use reflection only where the class cannot be known at compile time (frameworks, plugins), and keep it out of hot paths.
cards.example:
java.util.function.Function<String,Integer> f = Integer::parseInt;
int direct = f.apply("42");
try {
  int viaReflection = (Integer) Integer.class.getMethod("parseInt", String.class).invoke(null, "42");
} catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 66 — when are native methods justified?
cards.back: Almost never — only for platform-specific facilities or legacy libraries not yet ported
cards.extra: JNI is unsafe, unportable and hard to debug. The book advises against it for performance.
cards.example:
class NativeRare {
    // Almost never: only platform-specific facilities or unported legacy libraries.
    native int platformFacility();
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 67 — what is the first rule of optimisation?
cards.back: Don't do it — measure first, and design clean code before tuning
cards.extra: Knuth's line opens the item. Optimising without measurement moves complexity into the wrong place.
cards.example:
long start = System.nanoTime();
java.util.List<Integer> xs = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) xs.add(i);
long elapsed = System.nanoTime() - start;
System.out.println(elapsed);

cards.front: Effective Java Item 68 — why follow naming conventions?
cards.back: They encode meaning: getX is a getter, isX returns boolean, MAX_SIZE is a constant
cards.extra: Consistency lets readers infer behaviour from the name. Violating it is a permanent tax on everyone who reads the code.
cards.example:
final class Names {
  static final int MAX_SIZE = 10;
  private int size;
  int getSize() { return size; }
  boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 69 — why should exceptions not drive normal control flow?
cards.back: They are slow, obscure the happy path, and can leave state half-updated
cards.extra: Use them for genuinely exceptional conditions. A loop that ends by throwing is a loop with the wrong exit condition.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
java.util.Map<String,String> m = new java.util.HashMap<>();
String v = m.get("a");
if (v != null) System.out.println(v);
try { v = m.get("missing").toString(); } catch (NullPointerException e) { v = null; }
int[] state = {0, 0}; state[0] = 1;
try { state[1] = Integer.parseInt("x"); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { /* half-updated */ }

cards.front: Effective Java Item 70 — when should an exception be checked and when unchecked?
cards.back: Checked for conditions the caller can recover from; unchecked (RuntimeException) for programming errors
cards.extra: A missing file is recoverable; a null argument is a bug. Getting this backwards makes APIs either noisy or unsafe.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
final class Net { void open(String h) throws java.io.IOException { throw new java.io.IOException(h); } }
try { new Net().open("host"); } catch (java.io.IOException e) { System.out.println("retry"); }
int age = -1;
if (age < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("age=" + age);

cards.front: Effective Java Item 71 — what is the cost of an unnecessary checked exception?
cards.back: Every caller must catch or declare it, even when they can do nothing about it
cards.extra: The book: if there is a reasonable way to prevent the condition, don't make it checked — return a value or throw unchecked.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
class CheckedCost {
    static void parse(String s) throws java.text.ParseException {
        new java.text.SimpleDateFormat().parse(s); // every caller must catch or declare it
    }
    void caller() { try { parse("x"); } catch (java.text.ParseException e) { throw new AssertionError(e); } }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 72 — why reuse standard exceptions?
cards.back: Callers already know them, and the API stays consistent with the platform
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
class StandardExceptions {
    static void check(String s, int n) {
        if (s == null) throw new NullPointerException("s");
        if (n < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative"); // standard types callers know
    }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 73 — what is exception translation?
cards.back: Catching a lower-level exception and throwing one expressed in your abstraction's terms
cards.extra: Leaking SQLException from a repository exposes implementation detail. Translate, and chain the cause so the original is not lost.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
class Translation {
    static String load(int id) {
        try { return java.nio.file.Files.readString(java.nio.file.Path.of("data-" + id)); }
        catch (java.io.IOException e) { throw new IllegalStateException("cannot load " + id, e); }
    }
}

cards.front: Effective Java Item 74 — how should you document exceptions?
cards.back: Declare each checked exception individually and describe the conditions with @throws
cards.extra: Declaring a superclass hides which failures are possible. The doc comment is the contract callers program against.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::03 Language Features::01 Exception Handling
cards.example:
final class Reader {
  /** @throws java.io.IOException if the file cannot be read
   * @throws IllegalArgumentException if path is blank */
  String first(String p) throws java.io.IOException { if (p.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("p"); throw new java.io.IOException(p); }
}
